descricao: Hair types, colors and styles; body and skin vocabulary; modifiers (quite, fairly, rather...); grooming phrases.

secoes.conteudo:
Here is a situation you probably know. Your friend is waiting for you at a busy coffee shop, and they call: 'I can't find you! Where are you?' You say 'I'm here!' That does not help. 'I'm the person... with a face...' Still nothing. What you need is the right vocabulary — words to describe what you look like, fast and clearly.

Describing appearance is one of the most practical skills in any language. We use it to find people in a crowd, to describe someone we just met, to remember someone from years ago. In English, this vocabulary comes up constantly — in conversation, in films, in books, everywhere.

In this material, you will learn the key words in pairs: each word alongside its opposite, always together. This is the fastest way to build vocabulary — you learn two words at the same time, and the contrast between them makes both stick. We will cover hair type, hair color, hair length, height, body shape, and skin — and then you will see how small words like **quite** and **fairly** turn simple descriptions into natural, fluent English.

secoes.titulo: Hair Type: Straight / Curly — with Wavy in Between
secoes.conteudo:
The shape of someone's hair is usually the first thing you notice. In English, three words cover the full range: **straight**, **wavy**, and **curly**. Think of these as three points on a spectrum.

At one end: **straight** hair. Straight hair falls flat and smooth, with no curves at all. It lies close to the head and moves as a single, clean shape. At the other end: **curly** hair. Curly hair forms tight, round spirals — the kind that spring back when you pull them. If you picture a phone cable from the 1990s, you have exactly the right image.

Right in the middle: **wavy** hair. Wavy hair is neither flat nor tightly coiled. It has gentle, flowing curves — like the letter S drawn loosely. Not straight enough to be called straight, not tight enough to be called curly. **Wavy** is the middle ground, and a lot of people fit there.

When you describe someone's hair type, these three words cover almost every situation. 'She has straight hair.' 'He has curly hair.' 'Her hair is wavy.' Notice how clean and complete these sentences are. No extra words needed — the word itself does all the work.

The straight / curly pair is especially useful because the contrast is so visual. Once you have seen it once, you never forget either word. And **wavy** becomes easy to remember too — it sits right between them, and you can almost feel the gentle movement in the word itself.

secoes.titulo: Color and Length: Fair / Dark, Long / Short
secoes.conteudo:
Once you know the shape of someone's hair, the next things to describe are its **color** and its **length**. These two details together give you a very complete picture in just a few words.

For color, the main pair is **fair** and **dark**. **Fair** hair is light in color — pale yellow, golden, or light honey tones. You might also hear the word **blonde**, which describes the same range. Both **fair** and **blonde** refer to light hair, and both are perfectly natural in English. At the other end of the spectrum: **dark** hair. **Dark** covers a wide range of deeper shades — brown, dark brown, and black. It is the standard, natural, polite word for darker hair, and it works in all contexts.

Then there is **grey** hair — or **silver**, if you want to sound more elegant. **Grey** is the color that comes with age. Calling it **silver** has a more distinguished, even admirable quality. 'She had beautiful silver hair' sounds very different from 'she had grey hair,' even though the color is exactly the same. These are the only two words you need — and the choice between them says something about the tone you want.

One very important note about the word **fair**: it does double duty. **Fair hair** means light-colored hair. **Fair skin** means light-colored skin. You will see it in both contexts constantly. It is worth learning now: fair always means light — whether for hair or skin.

For **length**, the pair is simple: **long** and **short**. Long hair reaches well past the neck; short hair is cut close to the head. In between, people say **medium-length** or simply **medium**. One specific length worth knowing: **shoulder-length** — hair that reaches exactly to the shoulders. Very common in real descriptions.

And speaking of length: the **ponytail**. A ponytail is a hairstyle where long hair is gathered and tied at the back of the head with a band, hanging down. It is such a recognizable image that the moment someone says 'she had her hair in a ponytail,' you know exactly what she looked like. Simple and precise — the best kind of vocabulary.

secoes.titulo: Height and Build: Tall / Short, Slim / Overweight
secoes.conteudo:
Now let's move from hair to the whole picture: how tall someone is and what shape their body has.

For **height**, the pair is simple: **tall** and **short**. Someone **tall** is above average height — their head is usually above the people around them. Someone **short** is below average height. Both words are direct and neutral. One thing worth noticing: **short** appears in two different contexts. Short hair = not long. Short height = not tall. Context always makes the meaning clear, but it is good to be aware of this from the start.

For **build** — the overall shape of someone's body — the main pair is **slim** and **overweight**. **Slim** describes someone who is pleasantly thin and looks healthy. It is almost always a positive word. When you call someone slim, it sounds like a compliment. At the other end: **overweight** — the polite, neutral, and appropriate term for someone who is heavier than average. It is simply a neutral description, without judgment.

Here is where things get interesting: there is a second word that means something very similar to slim — **thin**. Both slim and thin mean 'not heavy,' but they do not feel the same. **Slim** always sounds positive. **Thin** is more neutral, and sometimes it even suggests concern — as if the person looks underweight or fragile. If you want to say someone looks good and healthy, use **slim**. If you are making a purely factual observation, or describing someone who looks unusually light, **thin** may be more accurate. Native speakers make this choice automatically. At B1 level, you should too.

Beyond the slim / overweight pair, there is one more word for build: **muscular**. **Muscular** describes someone with strong, developed muscles — the kind you build from training regularly. It sits on a different axis from slim and overweight. A muscular person can also be slim. It is simply an extra detail about the shape and strength of the body.

secoes.titulo: Skin: Pale / Tanned — and What 'Dark' Really Means
secoes.conteudo:
Describing skin in English is clear once you have three words: **pale**, **tanned**, and **dark**.

The most interesting pair is **pale** and **tanned** — because they describe the same type of person in two different conditions. **Pale** skin is light-colored skin that does not get much sun. Think of someone who works indoors, lives somewhere cold, or simply burns rather than tans. 'She has very pale skin.' 'He looked pale after a long winter.'

**Tanned** skin is pale skin that has become darker because of sun exposure. It is not someone's natural color — it is a temporary change from time in the sun, at the beach, or on holiday. 'He came back from Portugal looking very tanned.' In British English, describing someone as tanned often carries a pleasant implication: outdoors, summer, holiday. The pair **pale / tanned** is especially useful because it describes the same person at different times of year. Same skin, different story.

Then there is **dark skin** — and this is different from tanned. **Dark** describes someone's natural skin color, not a change from the sun. 'She has dark skin' is simply a neutral color description, exactly like 'She has dark hair.' It covers a wide range of naturally darker skin tones and is always appropriate and respectful in English.

One more word, used mostly in British English: **spotty**. **Spotty** means skin with spots or pimples — acne. It is casual and everyday. Teenagers know this word well. There is no strong opposite for spotty — you would simply say 'clear skin' or 'smooth skin.'

Here is the section that will make your English sound much more natural and real. Native speakers almost never say just 'she is tall' and leave it there. They add a small word before the adjective to show how strong the description is. These words are called **modifiers**, and they are everywhere in real English.

The modifiers you need to know are: **really**, **very**, **so**, **quite**, **fairly**, **pretty**, and **rather**. Let's look at each group.

**Really**, **very**, and **so** make an adjective stronger. 'She is really tall.' 'He is very muscular.' 'Your hair is so curly!' These feel natural and common in everyday conversation. **So** in particular adds emotion. When you say 'so,' you mean it — you are a little surprised or impressed. 'She is so slim!' carries more feeling than 'She is very slim.'

Now the interesting ones: **quite**, **fairly**, **pretty**, and **rather**. These four words all soften an adjective — they mean 'not completely, but a noticeable amount.' They are all similar, but each has its own personality.

**Quite** is the most common and neutral. 'She is quite slim' means she is slim, but you are being calm and measured. 'He has quite long hair' is a simple, polite observation. **Fairly** sounds a little more careful. 'She is fairly tall' means she is tall, but not unusually so. **Pretty** — and here is the important part — when used as a modifier, **pretty** has nothing to do with 'beautiful.' It simply means 'quite' or 'rather a lot.' 'She is pretty short' means she is noticeably short. This use of **pretty** is very common in American English, so you will hear it constantly in films and series. And **rather** sounds a bit more British and sometimes suggests mild surprise. 'He was rather thin' feels like 'hm, thinner than I expected.'

Here are some real example sentences: 'She was quite slim.' 'He has pretty curly hair.' 'I am fairly tanned.' 'She was rather pale.' All of these sound completely natural. This is the kind of English that makes people think: wow, your English is really good.

Beyond describing how people look, we also need to talk about the things people do to change or take care of their appearance. This vocabulary is very useful in everyday life — and it also gives you good practice with the present continuous.

To **get a haircut** means to go to a hairdresser and have your hair cut. 'I need to get a haircut' is a sentence you will hear and use all the time. To **brush your hair** means to use a brush to make your hair neat and smooth. To **comb your hair** is the same idea, but with a comb — the thin tool with small teeth, usually used for shorter or straighter hair.

To **shave** means to remove hair with a razor. Men often shave their face in the morning. 'He shaves every day.' To **put on makeup** means to apply cosmetics — things like foundation, lipstick, and mascara. 'She puts on makeup before work.' And to **get dressed** means to put on your clothes. 'I need to get dressed' might be the most common morning sentence in the English language.

All of these phrases work naturally in the present continuous — the form we use for actions happening right now. 'He is shaving.' 'She is brushing her hair.' 'They are getting dressed.' You already know this tense, so this is a great opportunity to use new vocabulary with a familiar structure. Two things at once — always a good deal.

Let's finish with a few words that are worth thinking about carefully — either because they have a similar word in Portuguese with a different meaning, or because they work differently from what you might expect.

First, and most important: **slim** and **thin**. In Portuguese, both translate to 'magro.' But in English, they are not the same. **Slim** = positive, healthy, a quiet compliment. **Thin** = neutral, sometimes a little concerning. If you want to say someone looks good, use **slim**. If you are simply observing that someone is not heavy — or that they look underweight — **thin** is more precise. Choosing the right one shows a real understanding of English nuance.

Second: **fair**. This word appears in many different parts of English life, and appearance is just one of them. In appearance: fair hair = light-colored hair, fair skin = light-colored skin. But fair also means just or equal: 'It's not fair!' It can mean good enough: 'The film was fair, not great.' And in weather: 'a fair day' means clear and pleasant. The word is the same; the context changes everything.

Third: **dark**. When describing appearance, **dark** is the natural, polite, and neutral word for both hair and skin in deeper shades. 'She has dark hair.' 'He has dark skin.' It is simply a color description. Portuguese speakers sometimes look for a more specific word, but in English, **dark** covers the full range and is always appropriate.

And finally: **tanned**. In Portuguese, you might say 'bronzeado.' In English, **tanned** describes exactly that — skin that has become darker because of sun exposure. It implies time outdoors or at the beach. 'He looks very tanned' often sounds like a compliment in English — it suggests an active, outdoor lifestyle. The key thing to remember: **tanned** is always a change from the sun, never someone's natural skin color. For natural color, the word is **dark**.
